title: Distilling Distributed ML Systems
summary: Distinguish the core focus of distributed ML systems engineering from foundational single-node model development.

blocks.md:
This lesson follows **Distilling Distributed ML Systems** in *Conclusion* (Vol II). By the end you should be able to:

- Distinguish the core focus of distributed ML systems engineering from foundational single-node model development
- Classify the four bands of the fleet stack and trace how physical limits propagate upward to bound serving and governance
- Evaluate why isolated component optimizations fail to guarantee end-to-end distributed system performance
- Analyze how non-compute bottlenecks (storage, fabric, governance) bind end-to-end production ML pipelines

blocks.source: Vol II, Conclusion, § Distilling Distributed ML Systems
blocks.md: A faster accelerator can finish its local work sooner yet leave the training job waiting on the same congested collective. Scale creates qualitative change because the binding constraint can leave the node. It moves into the fabric that carries gradients, into the recovery machinery that restores state after routine failure, into the service contract that decides whether capacity reaches users in time, and into the obligations that decide whether the service may run at all.

blocks.title: Map of the section
blocks.md: Pay attention to: the qualitative shift from single-node ML to distributed production; the fleet stack as an organizing framework across infrastructure, distribution, deployment, and governance; cross-layer constraint coupling where non-compute bottlenecks bind end-to-end throughput.

blocks.prompt: Think first: Explain why any single constraint in the fleet stack, such as a slow storage checkpoint or an unmeasured governance requirement, can bind the entire production pipeline, even when compute accelerators operate at peak utilization.
blocks.md: Distributed ML systems operate as a coupled chain of interdependent rates and operational obligations. A blocking synchronous checkpoint pauses the participating training workers while it completes. Asynchronous checkpointing can overlap writes with useful work, but exposed pauses, resource contention, and incomplete durable state still constrain progress and recovery. In serving, fabric congestion or queuing tail effects convert high raw FLOP throughput into unacceptable user-visible latency. At the governance layer, failing to establish data provenance, privacy bounds, or fairness auditing can legally or operationally block deployment regardless of technical performance. Thus, the system is bounded by its tightest operational constraint, not its fastest compute resource.

questions.q: A team transitions an ML model from single-node workstation experimentation to a multi-data-center production service handling 50,000 queries per second with high-availability and regulatory compliance requirements. According to the chapter's synthesis, which shift in engineering focus best characterizes this transition?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is B. Extending single-node reasoning about models, data pipelines, execution, and deployment to coupled fleet infrastructure, data center fabrics, distributed protocols, automated fault recovery, and governance frameworks. The section establishes that single-node ML engineering already couples models, data pipelines, execution, and deployment constraints. Distributed ML engineering extends that reasoning across shared infrastructure, distributed protocols, and fleet governance. The answer describing CUDA kernel compilation focuses on low-level single-device acceleration rather than fleet-scale infrastructure. The choice regarding symbolic loss optimization misidentifies training mathematics as a distributed systems shift. The option suggesting that fine-tuning eliminates network synchronization is false, as distributed fine-tuning across clusters still requires communication and collective synchronization.

questions.q: In a distributed ML system, optimizing individual layers in isolation (such as independently maximizing storage IOPS, network bandwidth, or serving concurrency) guarantees optimal end-to-end system throughput.
questions.explanation: False. In distributed ML systems, the layers are coupled rates and constraints. A local optimization that improves one component can be completely negated if another layer binds the system (for example, high storage read bandwidth is wasted if collective communication saturates the network fabric). End-to-end system optimization requires cross-layer co-design and matching rates rather than isolated layer improvements.
